segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter and the other disciple set out and were going to the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came to the tomb first,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and bending down to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Simon Peter also came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the face cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up separately, in a place of its own.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the other disciple, who had come to the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they did not yet understand the scripture, that he must rise from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the disciples went back again to their homes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Mary stood outside by the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had been lying, one at the head and one at the feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to her,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Woman, why are you weeping?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have put him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, if you have carried him off, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him away.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Mary.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She turned and said to him in Aramaic,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbouni!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which means Teacher).

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have seen the Lord,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that he had said these things to her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were locked where the disciples were, for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Peace be with you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to them again,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I am sending you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he breathed on them and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Receive the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven them; if you retain anyone’s, they are retained.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Thomas, one of the Twelve, the one called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the other disciples kept telling him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have seen the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the mark of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will never believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Eight days later his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Though the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Peace be with you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to Thomas,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Bring your finger here and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side. Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thomas answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My Lord and my God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and so that by believing you may have life in his name.

notes.note: The Greek does not say what the disciple believed. Most interpreters take it as the first faith that Jesus had risen, with the next verse explaining that this faith came from what he saw and not yet from an understanding of Scripture. A minority view, found already in antiquity, is that he simply believed Mary's report that the body was gone.

The Greek word means 'in the language of the Hebrews' and was used in this period without distinguishing Hebrew from Aramaic, the related language most Jews of Judea and Galilee spoke every day. 'Rabbouni' is an Aramaic form, so 'in Aramaic' is used here. Older translations and some current ones have 'in Hebrew'; others make the same choice as this one. Jesus also addresses Mary by the Semitic form of her name, Mariam.

notes.phrase: Do not hold on to me
notes.note: The verb can mean either 'touch' or 'take hold of, cling to'. The form of the command used here often means 'stop doing' something already under way. Most modern translations therefore have 'do not hold on to me' or 'do not cling to me' in place of the older 'touch me not'. The sense is that Mary must not try to keep him as he was, since he is on his way to the Father. How the reason given ('for I have not yet ascended') fits the command remains debated.

The Greek is literally 'the Jews'. The disciples behind the locked doors are themselves Jews, so the word here refers to the Jerusalem authorities who had brought about Jesus's execution, as it often does in John. Scholars are divided on how to render the term in this Gospel: some keep 'the Jews' throughout, and others prefer 'Judeans'.

This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and when breath enters the slain in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). A reader who knew those passages would hear an act of new creation. The Greek word for 'Spirit' also means 'breath'.

The verbs 'are forgiven' and 'are retained' are in the Greek perfect tense, which describes a settled state. Some take this to mean 'they have already been forgiven', so that the disciples declare what God has done; most read it as stating the standing result of the disciples' act. The grammar alone does not decide the question, and the verse has been understood differently across Christian traditions.

Didymos is the ordinary Greek word for 'twin', and a Greek reader would have heard it as a meaning and not as a foreign name. 'Thomas' itself reflects the Aramaic word for 'twin', so John is translating the name for his readers. Translations are divided between 'Didymus' and 'the Twin'.
Ancient counting usually included both the first and the last day. 'After eight days' therefore means a week later, on the following first day of the week.

notes.phrase: Do not be unbelieving, but believing
notes.note: The Greek sets two matching adjectives side by side, apistos and pistos, 'unbelieving' and 'believing', and the rendering keeps the pair. Several modern translations have 'do not doubt but believe' or 'stop doubting and believe', which is the source of the phrase 'doubting Thomas'. The Greek has no word for doubt here; Thomas had flatly refused to believe (verse 25).

notes.phrase: Have you believed because you have seen me?
notes.traditional: Because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, so the words can be read as a question or as a statement ('Because you have seen me, you have believed'). The edition translated here punctuates it as a question, as do several modern translations. Either way the remark is a mild contrast with those who believe without seeing, not a rejection of Thomas's confession.

The manuscripts differ by one letter between two forms of the verb. One naturally suggests 'may go on believing' and the other 'may come to believe'. The edition translated here prints the first. The choice bears on whether the Gospel was written mainly to strengthen believers or to win new ones, though many scholars doubt the verb form alone can settle that.

The Greek christos is here a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the claim is that Jesus is that figure. 'Messiah', from the Hebrew equivalent, conveys the title to a modern reader, for whom 'Christ' sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in passages like this while keeping 'Christ' where it functions as a name.

candidates.reason: Recurs in John and Revelation (and compare Acts' 'Hebrew dialect'), sometimes with Aramaic words and sometimes with Hebrew ones, so 'in Hebrew' versus 'in Aramaic' needs one policy.
A key Johannine term also common in the Synoptics and Acts; translators vary between 'sign', 'miracle' and 'miraculous sign', and variation would hide John's theme.

candidates.rendering: Sir (vocative to a supposed stranger); Lord (of Jesus)
candidates.reason: The vocative ranges from polite 'sir' to confessional 'Lord' across the Gospels, and the line between them needs a consistent rule.
With sins or debts it recurs throughout the New Testament and could be rendered 'forgive', 'release' or 'remit'; readers should see one choice.
As a form of address (John 2:4, 4:21, 19:26, 20:13, 15; Matthew 15:28) it was courteous in Greek but sounds brusque in English, so a single policy with a standing note is needed.
